articles.title: Couple bought a £1.2 million home with a dog-proof fence; years later, neighbours claimed half an acre of their garden
articles.summary: Rest of World News: David Todd and Caroline Hodge bought their £1.2 million home in East Sussex with a countryside setting and a secure fence that was important because t.
articles.body: David Todd and Caroline Hodge bought their £1.2 million home in East Sussex with a countryside setting and a secure fence that was important because they owned two Labradors. Years later, however, that same fence became the centre of a dispute with their new neighbours. The disagreement focused on about half an acre of land that Todd and Hodge believed was part of their garden. Their neighbours argued that the land belonged to them, based on the legal boundary recorded for the property.The £1.2 million home and its disputed dog-proof fence According to The Independent, David Todd, 69, and Caroline Hodge, 65, bought Wyland Wood near Robertsbridge, East Sussex, for around £1.2 million in 2018. This 19th-century detached stone house has four bedrooms and three bathrooms and sits within 2.7 acres of gardens and woodland. It also has a drawing room, a dog and boot room and a treehouse.The couple had particular reason to value the fencing around the property. The Independent reported that estate agents had assured the couple that the garden was enclosed by a dog-proof fence, something they considered important because they owned two Labradors. Hodge described the dogs as their sweethearts during the earlier court proceedings.At the time they bought the property, the fence was already in place and appeared to provide a clear physical edge around the garden. The couple later argued that they reasonably believed everything inside it was part of the property they were purchasing.The situation changed after Richard Marsh, 44, and his wife Rebecca, 40, bought neighbouring ancient woodland and an adjoining meadow in May 2021, as reported by The Independent.What changed after the Marshes bought the neighbouring landThe disagreement began when the Marshes determined that the existing fence did not match the boundary shown in the Land Registry records. They maintained that about half an acre inside the fence actually belonged to them, along with an important strip providing access to their land.The Independent reported that Marsh then began removing sections of the existing fence and intended to put up a new one along the boundary shown on the property documents. Todd and Hodge objected, saying this would take part of what they understood to be their garden.The couple obtained a court injunction requiring Marsh to stop removing the fence, preventing him from putting up a replacement and requiring sections that had already been removed to be restored.The disagreement eventually reached court, where the question was not simply where the visible fence stood, but which line legally represented the boundary between the two properties.How did the courts determine where the boundary layAt the 2025 county court hearing, Judge Caroline Parker ruled in favour of the Marshes. According to The Independent, she found that sections of the dog-proof fence stood between 6 and 8 metres outside the paper boundary of the land.That boundary was identified by a tree line and remnants of an older wire fence. The judge accepted that Todd and Hodge believed the existing fence marked the edge of their garden and noted that it was more obvious on the ground than the tree line.However, the court decided that describing the garden as dog-proof in the estate agent’s particulars was not enough to establish that the fence represented the legal boundary.The judge also ruled that the disputed half acre could be fenced off by the Marshes. They were awarded £3,174 in damages. The ruling meant that the couple lost a sizable section of the garden they had believed came with Wyland Wood.The couple challenged the original ruling based on the previous ownerTodd and Hodge appealed the decision, arguing that a reasonable purchaser would have understood the visible fence to mark the property's boundary.They also relied on a separate argument involving the previous owner of the Marshes’ land, Stephen Baldwin. The couple said emails exchanged with Baldwin while discussing repairs to the fence, amounted to a boundary agreement. Their position was that the correspondence showed the land inside the fence belonged to Wyland Wood.According to The Independent, Todd’s barrister argued that a boundary agreement could arise even without a formal dispute about the boundary. The couple’s case was that the existing fence had been treated as the boundary during discussions about repairing it.The Marshes rejected that interpretation. Their barrister argued that the emails were about sharing repair costs rather than agreeing where the property boundary stood.What did the High Court decide about the half acreIn July 2026, the High Court dismissed Todd and Hodge’s appeal, according to The Independent. Mr Justice Michael Green upheld the earlier decision that the legal boundary was the one shown on the registered title plans and historical property documents, rather than the dog-proof fence.The court noted that the fence ran parallel to the paper boundary but stood between 6.37 metres and 11.37 metres on the Marshes’ side of it.The judge also rejected the claim that the emails with Baldwin created a boundary agreement. The discussions had concerned repairs to the fence, rather than its precise legal position. The court found that Baldwin had not consciously considered the boundary when agreeing to share repair costs.As a result, the long-running dispute ended with the paper boundary remaining in place. The fence that had helped Todd and Hodge feel their dogs and garden were secure could not be treated as the legal dividing line between the properties.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Houthi drone debris kills one, injures two in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Middle East News: Saudi Arabia said on Thursday that debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed one person and injured two others in Taif, as fighting between the I.
articles.body: Saudi Arabia said on Thursday that debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed one person and injured two others in Taif, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group, Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and their allies intensified amid the wider Middle East conflict.Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence said the falling debris caused “one death, two injuries, and material damage to several buildings and vehicles”. The person killed was a Yemeni national, while the injured included a Saudi citizen and a Pakistani resident, according to Saudi authorities.The incident came a day after Riyadh said it had intercepted a drone headed towards Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca, while Iran’s Foreign Ministry urged against using claims over drone interceptions to escalate tensions.The renewed violence follows the collapse of a fragile truce in Yemen and a fresh Houthi offensive that has seen the group make gains along the Red Sea coast. Reuters reported that thousands of Yemenis were fleeing by sea as fighting intensified, with more than 100,000 people displaced by the renewed conflict.The strategic stakes have also widened beyond Yemen. The Houthis have taken control of areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s key maritime chokepoints, raising concerns over shipping and energy supplies. Reuters said the group’s gains had increased risks around a route critical to global trade.On Thursday, the Houthi-backed Almasirah television reported that Saudi warplanes had struck telecommunications towers in Taiz province, killing one civilian and injuring another. It also reported that three children were killed in strikes by forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government. Those claims could not be independently verified.Saudi Arabia’s latest casualties have also placed renewed attention on its defence arrangements with Pakistan and Turkiye. The three countries recently signed a defence pact, while Pakistan has said the agreement could become operational in the event of aggression against Saudi Arabia.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: RANDOM MUSING | DIVIDED KINGDOM? Why Scotland, Wales and Ireland want to 'leave' the UK
articles.summary: UK News: Explore the growing movements in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland for independence from the UK, spurred by Brexit and recent political statements from Donald Trump. What does this mean for the future of the United Kingdom?
articles.body: The Partition of India — and before it the Partition of Bengal — were among the most consequential acts of British imperial cartography, with the former leaving countless dead, a subcontinent in perennial trauma and perhaps even helping create some of the geopolitical conditions from which pan-global Islamist terrorism later emerged with a little help from Uncle Sam. Ergo, there is a little schadenfreude in seeing talk of partition engulf the country that facilitated it: the United Kingdom, or should we call it the Divided Kingdom?The latest shot comes from the person whose logorrhoea has truly upended the world order carefully put in place after the Second World War. Speaking in Ireland, Donald Trump put the fat in the fire by saying he would “love” to see a “united” Ireland, saying it was inevitable and “may as well happen now”. UK PM Andy Burnham – who, if you squint your eye, looks like an AI-generated image of Keir Starmer – pushed back, only for Trump to double down and call it “pretty cool”.Now, for Trump, saying something is “pretty cool” could be as serious as toppling a Supreme Leader or having regular Coke instead of Diet Coke, but his statement certainly caused some excitement.Now here’s the reason why Trump’s rhetoric is a little more than just words.For perhaps the first time in their history, Ireland, Scotland and Wales are led by parties and politicians who want to change their nations’ relationship with the UK, a sort of Brexit, if you will, except this was never how Brexit was supposed to work.The Brexit Referendum in 2016, which is as hackneyed as Yes Minister’s British sausage plot to get Jim Hacker elected as PM, has consumed six Prime Ministers, effectively turning 10 Downing Street into an AirBNB.Instead of freeing the UK from the bureaucrats in Brussels, it has instead put a man who recently beat a novelty candidate wearing a trash can within touching distance of the Prime Minister’s seat. And now it has created a political situation where the UK might finally become “divided”. Britain has survived the Spanish Armada, Napoleon, two world wars, the loss of empire, the Troubles, Brexit and even Meghan Markle — but it might not survive Donald Trump.Scotland wants independence, Plaid Cymru (Wales’ governing party) is toying with the idea, and Sinn Fein wants Northern Ireland to leave one state and join another.In Ted Lasso, the Panglossian protagonist once asked: “How many countries are in this country?” And to explain that properly, we have to go back to the World Cup quarter-final when England faced Erling Haaland and Norway. In a way, Haaland’s predecessors, the Vikings, are responsible for what we call the United Kingdom. Unlike Haaland and his compatriots, who weren’t that successful while raiding the English defence, his predecessors attacked so much that the warring Anglo-Saxon tribes had to band together under Alfred the Great before Æthelstan put together what can be recognised as the first united England.Once it had set its own affairs in order, England turned to its neighbours, conquering Wales. The neighbour that gave the most trouble — and not just because of Mel Gibson’s antisemitic views — was Scotland, which continued to resist England.Edward I tried, William Wallace resisted, Robert the Bruce won at Bannockburn in the first Spiderman prequel and Scotland remained sovereign. And then in 1603 the joke wrote itself when James VI of Scotland inherited England. No invasion was needed, but the two kingdoms retained separate parliaments and laws, perhaps because the Scots were always wary of the English.That arrangement spectacularly imploded under James’s son Charles I, whose quarrels with Parliament eventually produced civil wars across England, Scotland and Ireland and ended with the rather permanent constitutional remedy of chopping off the king’s head. Ireland was already deeply entangled in the mess after the rebellion of 1641, and when Oliver Cromwell crossed the Irish Sea in 1649, he ended up causing far more damage than the Dothraki and the Unsullied did on Westeros.Abolishing the monarchy, Lord-Protector Cromwell briefly pulled England, Scotland and Ireland into one republican experiment which was as successful as the MAGA Republican experiment. Cromwell’s Puritan regime was so maudlin that the entire kingdom decided that it was considerably less irritating to have a Crown than a prude in charge.While the monarchy returned with Charles II, the constitutional problem remained as all three countries continued to behave on their own. The marriage between England and Scotland began properly in 1707 because England wanted a common Protestant succession and Scotland’s elite wanted to dip their fingers into the giant and ever-expanding pie that was the English colonial markets. The Acts of Union created Great Britain, and Scots subsequently became energetic participants in the British Empire.Ireland, however, kind of like Roy Keane in his last days at Manchester United, continued to rage. It had been under varying degrees of English control for centuries, beginning with the Anglo-Norman invasion, through the Tudor conquest and Cromwell’s campaigns. It still remained a separate kingdom, and after the 1798 rebellion and with the French making eyes, London decided enough was enough. While the Irish Commons initially rejected the offer, palms were greased with peerages, pensions and patronage to create the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.Like Roy Keane at Manchester United after his epic MUTV rant, the arrangement didn’t last, with Irish nationalism, the Easter Rising and the War of Independence eventually producing the Anglo-Irish Treaty, and in 1922 most of Ireland chose Brexit while Northern Ireland remained.As the empire crumbled under its own guilt, Westminster tried devolution, with the Scots getting a parliament, Wales an assembly and the Good Friday Agreement creating power-sharing in Northern Ireland in an awkward situationship in which, if a majority of Northern Ireland wanted it, it could become a part of a united Ireland.And things roiled on, despite the fireworks brought by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) – seldom referred to as terrorists because they are white – ending with the aforementioned Good Friday Agreement in 1998. IRA’s political wing Sinn Fein was admitted into the multi-party peace talks and by 2005 the IRA put down its arms, realising there were better ways to make noise.And then came Brexit, in which Scotland voted heavily to Remain, Northern Ireland voted Remain, while Wales voted Leave alongside England.Now Scotland has the most mature independence movement, with the SNP holding 58 and the pro-independence Greens 15, giving them 73 in a 129-seat assembly.While Scotland has a fair degree of freedom with its own parliament and legal system, foreign affairs, immigration and monetary policy are still decided in Westminster. Now Scottish independence enthusiasts argue that leaving the UK would allow Scotland to pull off its own reverse Brexit and rejoin the EU, which would be better for Scottish economic policy and allow it to have its own affairs.Meanwhile, the unionists – those who want things to remain as they are – and who, funnily enough, are the most hardcore Trump supporters, argue that the fiscal deficit would make it difficult, and with independence would come arguments about tax, spending, debt, and basically that adulting will be too expensive, something every youngster learns once they leave their parents’ house.Wales, on the other hand, the least insouciant of the English neighbours, has Plaid Cymru in charge. The desire for independence is less than Scottish levels, and while it has ruled out a referendum, it argues that Wales could have a whale of a time if it possessed a little more freedom.And Northern Ireland’s break for freedom is more Winky than Dobby, because Sinn Fein isn’t proposing a new country: it just wants reunification with an existing EU member state.Of course, none of this could have happened without Brexit, which, with the benefit of hindsight, tells us that one shouldn’t leave the fate of a nation to overgrown public schoolboys who have to remain tight-lipped about hogs to call referendums that really aren’t needed. Despite a majority after many years of torrid Tory misrule, Labour is hurtling from one disaster to another and looks set to say ‘fare thee well’ if an election was held. But perhaps the biggest irony was Nigel Farage, Donald Trump’s most beloved British politician, who loves crypto as much as his special friend, having to break from his MAGA buddy to insist that Northern Ireland will remain an integral part of the UK.The irony is quite delicious because Great Britain has spent many centuries drawing borders, joining kingdoms, partitioning countries and deciding what flag will flutter over people’s heads. At one time it had an empire so vast that the sun didn’t set on it. Whether the United Kingdom becomes divided is ultimately for the people living in its constituent nations to decide – a right that many who were ruled by Great Britain never had – but for those of us who lived under the yoke of colonial rule, there’s a certain historical irony in watching Britain discover it’s considerably less fun when someone draws and redraws borders based on their own fancies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Two Washington entrepreneurs started a dog-waste cleanup business with about $1,000; six years later, Swoop Scoop says the operation generates more than $200,000 a month across multiple markets
articles.summary: US News: What started as a small Washington business built around one of the least glamorous chores of dog ownership has grown into a multi-market operation ge.
articles.body: What started as a small Washington business built around one of the least glamorous chores of dog ownership has grown into a multi-market operation generating more than $200,000 a month. William Milliken and Levi Swartz founded Swoop Scoop in late 2020 in Spokane Valley, Washington, after recognising that picking up dog waste was an overlooked service that many pet owners would gladly outsource. According to the episode of Millionaire University, featuring Swoop Scoop president Milliken, the entrepreneurs started the business with about $1,000 and grew it from roughly 20 customers to more than 300 within just a few months. In the episode, Milliken says the company now generates more than $200,000 a month and has expanded into multiple markets. Swoop Scoop's own website describes the company as a dog-waste removal service created to make life easier for pet owners and says it now serves customers across multiple markets.From a simple chore to a business ideaThe concept behind Swoop Scoop was straightforward. Milliken and Swartz had both spent years cleaning up after their own dogs and recognised an opportunity in a chore that was necessary but rarely enjoyable. Rather than creating a new product, the founders focused on providing a service. Customers could pay someone else to regularly remove dog waste from their yards, turning an unpleasant household task into a recurring business relationship.According to Swoop Scoop, the company was founded in late 2020 in Spokane Valley with the goal of eliminating what it describes as one of the most dreaded chores for dog owners. The company says its founders recognised that professional pooper-scooping was an overlooked service across the United States. That basic idea became the foundation for a business that could grow one customer and one neighbourhood at a time.Starting with about $1,000The company's beginnings were modest. Milliken told Millionaire University that he and Swartz started Swoop Scoop with about $1,000. The business then grew rapidly, with the podcast reporting that its customer base expanded from roughly 20 customers to more than 300 in a matter of months. The founders used relatively straightforward marketing methods to attract customers. Milliken discusses Facebook advertising in the podcast, along with the importance of recurring subscription revenue to the company's model.That recurring element is particularly important for a service such as dog-waste removal. A customer who signs up for regular cleaning can generate repeated revenue rather than providing the company with only a single transaction. The podcast describes this as part of the appeal of so-called “boring” businesses, where a simple service can create a dependable customer relationship without requiring a large initial investment.Why dog-waste removal can scaleDog-waste removal may not sound like a conventional high-growth business, but its simplicity can also make the model relatively easy to replicate. A worker does not need to manufacture a product or maintain a large inventory. The company instead organises routes, schedules recurring visits and provides the service at customers' homes.Swoop Scoop's current website shows how the original idea has developed into a broader service business. The company says it provides dog-waste removal and has built a team focused on delivering what it describes as a professional, “white glove” experience for customers. The company has also expanded geographically. Its website lists service areas including Spokane, Seattle, Everett and North Idaho, reflecting its growth beyond the Spokane Valley market where it began.Expanding beyond SpokaneThe expansion accelerated as Swoop Scoop built its customer base and operations. In 2023, the company, then known as Scoop Troop, acquired Dooky's Pet Waste Removal for $54,000, according to the Spokane Journal of Business. At the time, the company had more than 1,500 customers and about a dozen employees and had expanded into Seattle.The company subsequently operated under the Swoop Scoop name as it continued developing its brand and expanding its reach. The company's growth has also been reflected outside its own reporting. Swoop Scoop was included on the 2025 Inc. 5000 list at No. 653, with Inc. reporting 638% three-year growth. A Spokane Journal of Business report on the Inc. 5000 recognition said the company's revenue had increased 638% between 2021 and 2024. It also reported that Swoop Scoop had locations in Seattle and Everett, Washington, and North Idaho.Building around recurring customersThe subscription model remains central to the company's approach. Instead of waiting for customers to call whenever their yards need cleaning, recurring services allow the company to schedule regular visits. That creates a predictable need for the customer and a repeat service opportunity for the business. The Millionaire University episode specifically identifies recurring subscription revenue as one of the reasons the business model is attractive. The podcast also discusses seasonal demand, expanding into new markets and knowing when to pivot as part of the challenges involved in growing the company.For Swoop Scoop, scaling therefore involves more than simply finding more people willing to scoop dog waste. It requires building routes, hiring and managing workers, maintaining customer relationships and entering new markets while keeping the service consistent.More than a dog-waste businessThe company's services have expanded beyond routine residential cleanups. Swoop Scoop's website describes its broader offering as including residential and commercial pet-waste removal, along with odour-control services. The company has also developed expertise around the business itself. Its broader ecosystem includes resources aimed at people interested in starting or growing businesses in the pet-waste-removal industry. That reflects how a service that began as a small local operation has evolved into a business model that the founders believe can be replicated in other markets.From $1,000 to more than $200,000 a monthThe numbers now associated with Swoop Scoop are far removed from its beginnings. The Millionaire University episode describes the company as a multi-million-dollar operation generating more than $200,000 every month. It also highlights the jump from roughly 20 customers to more than 300 within a few months and the company's expansion into multiple markets. Meanwhile, the company's own website documents its origins, its expansion into multiple markets and its focus on making dog ownership easier by taking over the task of waste removal.The Swoop Scoop story illustrates how a business does not necessarily need an elaborate product or a huge starting investment to find a market. Two entrepreneurs began with about $1,000 and a service built around a chore many people would rather avoid. Six years later, their company says it has grown into a multi-market operation generating more than $200,000 a month, turning an ordinary household nuisance into the foundation of a sizeable business.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Anna’s hummingbirds were absent from Portland before 1968, but today they are among the city’s most common birds after expanding north
articles.summary: US News: Anna’s hummingbirds have expanded their range across the Pacific Northwest, with a presence in cities such as Portland, Oregon. Once largely associate.
articles.body: Anna’s hummingbirds have expanded their range across the Pacific Northwest, with a presence in cities such as Portland, Oregon. Once largely associated with California, the small, colourful birds gradually moved north and established populations in Oregon, Washington and British Columbia. Records show that numbers remained low for decades before rising rapidly from the late 1990s. Today, Portland has an estimated abundance of 2.01 Anna’s hummingbirds per party-hour, placing it alongside cities in northern California. Researchers link the expansion to population growth, introduced plants, ornamental gardens and hummingbird feeders, while climate change may have helped the species colonise some colder areas.Portland’s Anna’s hummingbirds took decades to spreadAccording to the study published in The University of Chicago Press, titled ‘Ecological Release of the Anna’s Hummingbird during a Northern Range Expansion’, the history of Anna’s hummingbirds in the Pacific Northwest is therefore not simply a story of birds arriving and immediately becoming abundant. The research found that populations in Oregon, Washington and British Columbia were present by the early 1970s, but they remained at low densities for decades. In the north-west, populations were consistently recorded from the mid-1960s, followed by a much faster rise from the late 1990s.Portland provides a striking example of how far that change went. In the study’s abundance estimates, Portland recorded 2.01 birds per party-hour, compared with 1.74 in Seattle, 1.92 in Oakland and 1.89 in San Jose. In other words, the Portland figure had reached levels comparable with cities in the northern part of the hummingbird’s historic range. The research also notes that populations in the Pacific Northwest show stronger growth than those in the species’ native range.Eucalyptus helped Anna’s hummingbirds expandEarlier increases in Anna’s hummingbird numbers in California were associated with the spread of introduced flowering plants, particularly eucalyptus. The trees provided nectar during periods when food could otherwise become scarce. Historical accounts cited by the study suggested that this helped support larger wintering populations.The research describes how hummingbird feeders and ornamental garden plants helped support newly established populations in areas where the species had previously been uncommon. A separate study cited by Battey found that Anna’s hummingbirds in their expanded northern range were more likely to visit feeders and use human-modified landscapes. The relationship could also reinforce itself: people who noticed hummingbirds were more likely to put up feeders, potentially increasing the food available to the birds.Climate change may have supported Northern ExpansionClimate change may have helped the birds colonise some northern locations, but the study does not identify it as the main explanation for the earliest stages of the expansion. Climate models based on conditions from 1895–1925 failed to predict the newly occupied areas of the Pacific Northwest. However, the researchers found that the area with minimum breeding-season temperatures suitable for the species increased by about 11% between 1895–1925 and 1995–2015.The birds have also adjusted their breeding schedule as they moved north. Nest records showed that the median nesting date in the Pacific Northwest was 11 days later than in California, while the beginning of the nesting season shifted by roughly 17–32 days in the comparison. The study concludes that Anna’s hummingbirds have become common breeding birds across the lowland Pacific Northwest by combining range expansion, changes in nesting timing and increasing use of human-modified habitats.Portland’s estimated abundance had reached 2.01 birds per party-hour, showing how a bird that was once unusual in the region had become a familiar part of the city’s birdlife.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: FBI warns ‘tradwife’ women may be targeting ICE agents through fake dating profiles: Report
articles.summary: US News: The FBI warned that a small group of women allegedly created fake online dating profiles using a “traditional wife” or “tradwife” image to attract US .
articles.body: The FBI warned that a small group of women allegedly created fake online dating profiles using a “traditional wife” or “tradwife” image to attract US immigration enforcement officers and expose their personal information online.The FBI’s Chicago office circulated a memo to law enforcement agencies in February about the alleged tactic, The Guardian reported, citing a document obtained through a public records request by government transparency nonprofit Property of the People.The memo said the women were allegedly creating fictitious dating profiles to attract and then “dox” law enforcement personnel involved in immigration enforcement.Fake profiles designed to attract officersAccording to the FBI briefing, the profiles used “traditional wife” imagery and listed specific interests intended to appeal to law enforcement personnel. The alleged objective was to lure officers into online or in-person interactions under the guise of a date and then publicly expose their identities and personal information.The FBI said the tactic was intended to cause public embarrassment and discourage immigration enforcement activity.However, the briefing did not identify the dating platforms allegedly used, specify where the women were based, or say whether any immigration officers had actually been exposed. The FBI also described the document as “not finally evaluated intelligence” and said it was issued to raise awareness about the alleged doxing technique.Property of the People obtained the memo through a public records request. The FBI memo came weeks after a New York Post report claimed that social media users were encouraging women to use dating apps to identify and expose ICE agents.That report cited posts from conservative account Libs of TikTok, but did not provide evidence that agents had actually been tricked.Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, criticised the FBI briefing, calling it a thinly sourced alert over alleged online dating attempts involving ICE agents.The FBI has issued other internal warnings about the doxing of immigration enforcement personnel. articles.title: No official dinners, foreign travel: Pakistan rolls out austerity measures amid fuel shock
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan on Thursday announced a fresh set of austerity measures, including a 50 per cent cut in fuel allocations for government vehicles and a ban on.
articles.body: Pakistan on Thursday announced a fresh set of austerity measures, including a 50 per cent cut in fuel allocations for government vehicles and a ban on official foreign travel and the purchase of new government vehicles. The measures come as rising global oil prices threaten fuel, gas and power supplies.The measures, approved by the Pakistan cabinet, will remain in force for three months as the government seeks to reduce fuel consumption and public expenditure.Under the new restrictions, markets will have to close by 9 pm, while marriage halls can operate until 10 pm and restaurants until 11 pm. Drug stores and medical laboratories have been exempted.Fuel allocations for government vehicles will be reduced by half, although vehicles used by the armed forces, law enforcement agencies and essential services will not be covered by the cut.The Shehbaz Sharif government has also ordered a five per cent reduction in non-employee-related expenditure and prohibited official foreign visits and domestic travel for meetings, directing officials to use virtual meetings instead.Official dinners have been banned, except those hosted for foreign visitors and delegations. The purchase of new government vehicles has also been prohibited, while procurement of durable goods has been restricted, with IT purchases exempted.The measures come two days after Pakistan raised petrol prices by PkR 4.10 per litre and high-speed diesel (HSD) by PkR 6.41 per litre. Petrol now costs PkR 384.34 per litre, while HSD is priced at PkR 415.83.Global oil prices have risen amid continuing conflict and supply concerns in West Asia, including attacks on energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the temporary closure of its East-West oil pipeline following an aerial attack.The austerity package is the second such effort this year. Pakistan introduced similar measures in March, including a temporary school shutdown, reductions in government fuel use and greater reliance on remote working.Earlier the government had introduced the Prime Minister's Fuel Relief Scheme from Wednesday, offering motorcycle, rickshaw and small-car owners a subsidy of 100 rupees (36 US cents) per litre on a capped monthly quota.The programme, however, has faced implementation difficulties. Karachi resident Mohammad Musharraf told Reuters: "First of all, you have to register your vehicle. Then you have to register your mobile phone. How can an illiterate person survive if the conditions are so difficult?"The energy pressures extend beyond transport. Reuters reported that Pakistan's power sector could require up to 400 million cubic feet of gas a day through winter, while only two LNG cargoes had been confirmed for September.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
